source: Vaccarino et al. (2026) Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis (DRAGO)
finding: LLM self-review of a runnable-but-wrong formal spec (SMT-LIB2, MiniZinc, PDDL) breaks correct artifacts. Replacing it with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis plus a rule that keeps a rewrite only if diagnosed error weight strictly falls cuts regressions to about one tenth.
numbers: Right-to-wrong regressions 1.3% (DRAGO) vs 11.8% (LLM diagnosis) of initially correct artifacts. Accuracy +12.9 pp over zero-shot, +8.7 pp over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged over 5 benchmarks, 4 models (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-Coder 30B, Gemma 4 31B).
limits: Formalism-specific checks must be hand-built per domain. Gain is small where zero-shot is at ceiling (Sonnet, 239 of 242 answerable). One config (Text2Zinc/Qwen) trailed LLM-diagnostic repair by 2.4 pts.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G2: revise only from real output, and gate acceptance on a check, not the model's opinion. Spec debugging is KB debugging.

source: Vaccarino et al. (2026) DRAGO, ablation of diagnosis vs gate
finding: Two parts matter separately. Grounded diagnosis helps more than the acceptance gate. Gating an LLM's own critique barely helps.
numbers: Holding the gate fixed, DRAGO beats LLM-diagnosis+gate in 16 of 20 configs, +7.1 pts on average, about +18 on ProverQA-hard. Removing the gate costs 5.1 pts FOL, 1.8 CSP, 0.9 PDDL. Gating LLM review adds only +1.1 pts. Solver-error-only repair: +10.7 pts on CSP, no gain on FOL/PDDL where wrong artifacts run cleanly.
limits: Three formalisms; effects differ by domain.
agent_relevance: A gate on a weak self-critique does not fix it. The diagnostic signal must be external. Execution errors alone are silent once code runs.

source: Vaccarino et al. (2026) DRAGO, per-case flips
finding: On PDDL, LLM self-review breaks more artifacts than it fixes; DRAGO fixes far more than it breaks.
numbers: Pooled over 2,400 paired rows: DRAGO 104 wrong-to-right vs 12 right-to-wrong; self-review 159 fixes vs 254 breaks. FOL (Haiku): baseline regression 7.7% FOLIO, 9.4% ProverQA-hard vs DRAGO 1.3% and 1.2%. Recovery 13.2% and 13.1% (DRAGO) vs 12.7% and 4.1% (baseline).
limits: Haiku FOL and pooled PDDL slices only for these figures.
agent_relevance: Count right-to-wrong flips as a first-class metric when testing any revise step.

source: Vaccarino et al. (2026) DRAGO, sampling comparison
finding: Sample-three-and-select is weaker than diagnose-and-repair. FOL, hosted models: zero-shot 78.6, sample-3 80.0, oracle-3 81.3, DRAGO 88.8.
numbers: FOL accuracy % as listed (Table 2).
limits: Only the FOL row was read in full.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: more samples from one model add little; a diagnostic check adds more.

source: Singha et al. (2025) Benchmark Dataset Generation and Evaluation for Excel Formula Repair with LLMs (FoRepBench)
finding: Microsoft built 618 validated faulty-Excel-formula repair samples (from 1,095 executable; 56% pass an LLM validator) and a baseline repair prompt. Real hand-curated faults are much harder than synthetic ones.
numbers: Execution match, FoRepBench vs seed (real) set: GPT-4.1 0.80 vs 0.41; GPT-4o 0.73 vs 0.35; Phi-3 0.58 vs 0.24; Mistral 0.51 vs 0.19. Cost about $0.026 per sample. LLM validator vs humans kappa 0.25.
limits: Single-sheet, English only; context truncated so distant and multi-sheet dependencies are lost. Synthetic faults are shallower and more local than real ones.
agent_relevance: Synthetic fault benchmarks overstate repair skill by roughly 2x. Test the agent on real faults.

source: Singha et al. (2025) FoRepBench, error structure
finding: Repair succeeds when logic is intact and only a local patch is needed (e.g. a VLOOKUP wrap). It fails when whole-logic rewrites or intent guesses are needed.
numbers: Synthetic-to-real drop in execution match: 0.39 (GPT-4.1) and 0.38 (GPT-4o). Larger GPT-4 series beat Phi-3 and Mistral.
limits: Authors' interpretation; no controlled test of which factor causes the gap.
agent_relevance: Local patch vs semantic rewrite is a useful split for deciding when to reframe.

source: Thorne (2025) Large Language Models for Spreadsheets: Benchmarking Progress and Evaluating Performance with FLARE
finding: 20 LLMs audited a small seeded-error spreadsheet (12 errors). Detection ranged 17% to 100%. Logic-formula errors were found best; surface data errors (typos, unit price 50 vs 500) were missed often.
numbers: Detected of 12: Gemini 2.5 Pro 12 (100%); ChatGPT-4.5 and o3-mini-high 11 (91.7%); Claude, ChatGPT-4 legacy, Grok3 10 (83.3%); GPT-4o-mini 2 (16.7%); Gemini Flash 3 (25%); Copilot 4 (33%).
limits: One spreadsheet, single run per model, no prompt variation; early-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Anomaly checks (typo, outlier) are missed by reasoning-only passes; give the agent a code check for them.

source: Thorne (2025) FLARE, Triangle spreadsheet
finding: On a classic EuSpRIG error-seeded challenge with 4 formula errors, many models detected none; only one model (MetaAI) fixed both the triangle inequality and the ORAND logic error.
numbers: Group A (score 0, no detections or fixes): DeepSeek R1, Perplexity, ChatGPT-4.5, o3-mini, Mistral and others. Best score 3 (MetaAI). Gemini 2.5 Pro fixed ORAND only, via min/max/median (score 1).
limits: Scoring is coarse; one task; illustrative.
agent_relevance: Even strong models miss logic faults without a localisation method.

source: Thorne (2023) Experimenting with ChatGPT for Spreadsheet Formula Generation: Evidence of Risk in AI Generated Spreadsheets
finding: ChatGPT writes correct formulas when the problem is clear and complete. With limited information or heavy multi-step logic it gives wrong formulas and false statements. Re-prompting fixed one omission but left a bracket-order error.
numbers: Qualitative case series, no sample statistics. On a contradiction logic puzzle only one conclusion (Saber asleep) was correct.
limits: Informal case study, GPT-3.5 era; no repeated runs.
agent_relevance: Fixing one fault by re-prompt can leave or create another: check after every revision.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) SpreadsheetBench 2: Evaluating Agents on End-to-End Business Spreadsheet Workflows
finding: Workflow-level benchmark, 321 tasks, 11.8 worksheets and 593.5 cell edits per task, 8 frontier models in one multi-turn agent scaffold. Debugging is the hardest category.
numbers: Debugging accuracy / cell-modification score: Claude Opus 4.6 12.00% / 50.38%; GPT-5.2 8.00% / 39.07%; Gemini 3.1 Pro 7.00% / 41.86%; DeepSeek-V3.2 10.00%; Qwen3.5-397B 3.00%. Overall best 34.89%. Debugging set 100 tasks.
limits: Accuracy needs every cell to match the golden file (strict); modification score shows partial credit.
agent_relevance: Locating the fault, not editing, is the bottleneck. Matches S5 needing real output that points at the fault.

source: Zhu et al. (2026) SpreadsheetBench 2, failure analysis
finding: Dominant failures are insufficient inspection and wrong target-cell selection. In debugging, agents spend over 60% of their trajectory inspecting (no step-by-step instruction given). Explicit error values (#REF!, #NUM!) are the hardest sub-type (best model barely above 20%).
numbers: Easier: incorrect index-match and incorrect sign. One weaker model (MiniMax M2.5) fixes individual errors in 34% of debugging runs but its final pass rate is 3%.
limits: Failure taxonomy from a sample of Claude Opus 4.6 failed trajectories only.
agent_relevance: A localise-then-edit split with explicit coverage of dependent cells targets the top failure modes.

source: Yang et al. (2026) SemLoc: Turning Free-Form LLM Reasoning into Executable and Verifiable Semantic Constraints
finding: LLM writes typed constraints at code anchors; these run as runtime checks over passing and failing tests (a violation spectrum); a counterfactual patch must pass all tests to count. LLM fault localisation becomes checkable evidence, like a spectrum plus a model.
numbers: Where coverage ties the faulty line: constraint violations rank it first in 40.9% vs 2.2% for SBFL and 7.0% for Daikon. 99.4% of constraints become checks. 68.4% of top answers have a test-confirmed patch and 93.6% of those are correct. Acc@1 81.4% vs 82.0% for an LLM given the same inputs (not significant) vs 50.0% for a function-only LLM. 809 real bugs, 750 projects; 4 LLMs.
limits: Needs tests as oracle; the ties-subset result is selective. Main gain is verifiability, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Model proposes, code checks and ranks.

source: Yang et al. (2026) SemLoc, confidence analysis
finding: The LLM's own stated confidence does not separate right from wrong localisations; counterfactual verification does.
numbers: LLMs report confidence of at least 0.9 for 76.2% of answers. Counterfactual verification: 68.4% verified, 93.6% correct; the unverified third holds about three quarters of the wrong answers. Only GPT-5.5 had confidence as informative as verification (95.6%). QuixBugs: Acc@1 74.2%, Acc@5 96.0%.
limits: Four LLMs; one differs from the rest.
agent_relevance: Confidence is a hint, a held-out check is proof (G3, G4).

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) A Quantitative and Qualitative Evaluation of LLM-Based Explainable Fault Localization (AutoFL)
finding: An LLM navigates a repo with function-call tools to localise bugs and explain them. Repeating the run and counting votes gives a confidence estimate.
numbers: 798 real bugs (Defects4J, BugsInPy). Method-level acc@1 vs Ochiai SBFL: +19.7% Defects4J, +166.7% BugsInPy (GPT-3.5), +233.3% BugsInPy (GPT-4). One GPT-4 run beats five aggregated GPT-3.5 runs. Five runs take 87.24 s vs 112 s reported for SBFL. 83.7% of individual runs gave correct explanations (Table 5).
limits: Benchmark memorisation risk; explanations cannot be self-consistency checked.
agent_relevance: Tool-navigated evidence plus repeated runs is a cheap locator; agreement is a hint, not proof (G4).

source: Rafi, Kim, Chen, Wang (2025) LLM4FL: Multi-Agent Fault Localization via Graph-Based Retrieval and Reflexion
finding: Three LLM agents with graph retrieval and Reflexion-style self-reflection improve Top-1 over AutoFL and SoapFL on Defects4J v2.0.0.
numbers: 675 faults. Top-1: LLM4FL 326, AutoFL 275 (+18.55%), AgentFL/SoapFL 311 (+4.82%). Top-3 +8.14% over AutoFL, +2.66% over AgentFL. Segmentation and prompt chaining add up to 22% Top-1.
limits: No isolated gain for the reflection step was read.
agent_relevance: Reflection loops give single-digit gains; compare to the larger gains from grounded checks.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Few-shot Self-Debugging: model explains its code line by line and uses execution results. Works without unit tests for text-to-SQL, better with them.
numbers: Spider (no unit tests): +2 to 3% with code explanation, +9% on hardest level. TransCoder and MBPP with unit tests: up to +12%. Matches or beats baselines that sample over 10x more candidates.
limits: Later work cited by DRAGO (Huang 2024, Stechly 2025) finds pure self-critique can hurt.
agent_relevance: The useful part is the real execution output (G2), not the explanation alone.

source: Luo et al. (2026) Rethinking Tool Design for Agentic RCA: A Controlled Empirical Study
finding: Controlled test of LLM agents with tools at three abstraction levels for root-cause analysis of microservice failures (375 cases, 3 systems, 8 configs). More tools do not reliably help; agents often override a correct tool-ranked candidate.
numbers: Qwen3.7-Plus top-1: L1 52.7%, L2 68.8%, L3 82.8%, raw-Python L0 85.4% (L3 uses under half the time). Type accuracy L0 41.4% vs full toolset 49.0%. The L3 candidate is correct in over 80% of trajectories, yet overrides outnumber corrections in every config; L2+L3 overrides 9.3% vs corrections 3.8%. Adding L3 to L1+L2 cuts Qwen3-8B AC@1 by 13.9 points because it calls L3 in 0.8% of runs vs 61.3-94.0% for larger models.
limits: Microservice RCA, Qwen family only.
agent_relevance: A diagnosis tool helps only if its result is used. Code, not the model, should decide whether a tool candidate is accepted.

source: Ao, Simchi-Levi, Wang (2026) ORLoopBench: Solver-in-the-Loop Benchmarks for Self-Correction (OR-Debug-Bench)
finding: Infeasible LP/MILP repair with Gurobi IIS (an irreducible infeasible subsystem, i.e. a minimal conflict set) as feedback each step: a direct model-based-diagnosis loop with LLMs. 5,362 instances, 26 models.
numbers: RR@5 (repaired within 5 steps) / diagnostic accuracy DA (overlap with true conflict set): Qwen3-8B-GRPO 95.3% / 62.4% / 2.25 steps; Claude Sonnet 4.6 92.4% RR@5; claude-sonnet-4 86.2% / 50.1%; o4-mini 86.2% / 47.8%; gpt-5.2-chat 81.8% / 40.9%; gemini-2.5-flash 70.7% / 19.2%. GRPO model +14.6 pp DA over o4-mini.
limits: The 8B model is RL-trained with solver reward (teachers GPT-5.2, o4-mini). High RR@5 with low DA means lucky repairs without understanding.
agent_relevance: IIS is a code-computed conflict set. Score a revise step on repair AND conflict coverage.

source: Ao, Simchi-Levi, Wang (2026) ORLoopBench, semantic drift and MILP
finding: Whole-model regeneration makes the solver say Optimal while solving the wrong problem. Constraint-level repair keeps the objective.
numbers: MILP drift test: GPT-5.4 Optimal in 90% but only 28.2% keep the correct objective; Claude Sonnet 4.6 85% Optimal vs 22.4% correct objective; Gemini 3.1 Pro 3% and 0.8%. MILP repair: LP-trained model zero-shot 78.8% RR@5; MILP-trained 87.1%; best API (Claude Sonnet 4.6) 71.0%.
limits: Single configurations per model.
agent_relevance: A pass from the executor is not proof (G3). Prefer minimal local edits over regeneration when revising.

source: Le, Tran, Lubos, Felfernig, Garber (2026) Early-Stage Product Line Validation Using LLMs
finding: 12 LLMs perform 16 feature-model analysis operations (dead features, void model, counts) on semi-formal text, compared with the solver FLAMA. Reasoning models approach solver accuracy but make systematic parsing and constraint-reasoning errors.
numbers: Average accuracy: Grok 4 Fast Reasoning 89.7%, GPT-5 mini 88.9%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 88.2%; reasoning-optimized 81.1% vs general-purpose 61.0%; Claude Sonnet 4 78.3%; Llama 4 Scout 42.7%. Runtime: FLAMA 18.45 s; DeepSeek Reasoner 9,508 s at 82.8%.
limits: Accuracy falls with blueprint size. A solver-free vs solver-style prompt comparison in the text (68.8 vs 56.0, 83.5 vs 79.2) was read from a flattened PDF and its direction is unverified.
agent_relevance: KB debugging by LLM alone is high but not solver-grade; keep a solver for guarantees.

source: Felfernig, Schubert, Zehentner (2012; arXiv 2021) An Efficient Diagnosis Algorithm for Inconsistent Constraint Sets (FastDiag)
finding: FastDiag finds one preferred minimal diagnosis by divide-and-conquer consistency checks, without computing conflict sets first. It is the main algorithm for diagnosing inconsistent knowledge bases and user requirements in configurators.
numbers: Evaluated on a bicycle configuration KB (about 65 constraints) and a computer-configuration dataset, N = 415 configurations. FastDiag beat QuickXplain-based hitting-set diagnosis in time to first diagnosis and top-5. Ranking differences significant (Mann-Whitney, p = 6.6e-5 between best-first and breadth-first HSDAG).
limits: Needs a strict preference order among constraints; exact speedup factors not read.
agent_relevance: A code-side routine for S5: find which constraint removal restores consistency, instead of asking the model.

source: Le, Vidal Silva, Felfernig, Benavides, Galindo, Tran (2023) FastDiagP: Parallelized Direct Diagnosis
finding: Parallelising FastDiag's consistency checks by speculative pre-computation speeds up diagnosis in large configuration KBs, but gains are modest.
numbers: Best at 8 cores; speedup 1.28 to 1.65 (runtime cut up to 40%). Linux-kernel configuration KB; more cores beyond 8 do not help.
limits: Speedup ceiling set by how many consistency checks are independent.
agent_relevance: Consistency checks dominate cost; budget them like model calls.

source: Cui et al. (2026) SymDiag: Explainable Diagnosis for LLM Reasoning via Neuro-Symbolic Verification
finding: Translates chain-of-thought into symbolic constraints and runs step-level SAT/entailment checks; returns unsat cores, counterexamples and missing premises for targeted repair. In an audited set 43.3% of traces were unfaithful and 25.0% had a correct answer on an unfaithful chain.
numbers: Faithfulness detection overall F1 70.7, above answer matching, LLM-as-Judge, reward models and LogicReward. Audited set 240 traces (136 faithful, 44 wrong, 60 correct but unfaithful). Up to 4 repair rounds beat all baselines. Removing step-level symbolic verification is the largest ablation drop.
limits: Preprint; NL-to-logic translation errors are a share of failures; uses GPT-OSS-120B as judge.
agent_relevance: Unsat-core style evidence localises the failing step; correct answers can sit on invalid steps.

source: Jannach and Schmitz (2016) Model-based diagnosis of spreadsheet programs: a constraint-based debugging approach
finding: Classical MBD for spreadsheets: formulas become constraints, test cases give conflicts, hitting sets give candidate faulty cells. Not opened this session; claim from background knowledge only.
numbers: Not read; no numbers recorded.
limits: Source not opened. Pointer only.
agent_relevance: Template for a code-side S5 localiser: formula-level components, conflicts from failing cells.

source: Huang et al. (2024); Stechly et al. (2025); Tyen et al. (2024), as cited by DRAGO on self-critique
finding: DRAGO cites these as showing LLM self-review misses errors, raises false alarms and corrupts correct answers. Their own tables were not opened; this line records only DRAGO's citation context.
numbers: No numbers read from these papers.
limits: Secondhand.
agent_relevance: Consistent with G2: models find errors poorly but fix well once shown.
